name: Hotta-Tanaka Shock Wave
description: The gravitational field of two massless particles in de Sitter space, the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole boosted to the speed of light with its energy held fixed. Spacetime is de Sitter on either side of a single null cone, a cosmological horizon, which carries an impulsive gravitational wave on a sphere of constant area with one particle at each pole.
convention: The de Sitter radius $a$ is a length, with $\Lambda = 3/a^2$, and we keep factors of $G$ and $c$ explicit. We read the Dirac delta $\delta$ as the limit of a pulse even about the shock, a prime on it a derivative with respect to its argument. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: What does gravity look like around a particle that moves at the speed of light through a universe with a cosmological constant? Peter Aichelburg and Roman Sexl had the answer for flat space by 1971: boost the Schwarzschild black hole ever faster while its mass goes to zero and its energy stays fixed, and the field flattens onto a single plane that travels with the particle [aichelburg1971]. The trick needs a boost, and de Sitter space has boosts of its own: drawn as the hyperboloid $-Z_0^2 + Z_1^2 + Z_2^2 + Z_3^2 + Z_4^2 = a^2$ in a flat space of five dimensions, it is carried into itself by every Lorentz transformation of the five [hotta1993]. Masahiro Hotta and M. Tanaka of Tohoku University wrote the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole on that hyperboloid, to first order in its mass, and boosted it along $Z_1$ [hotta1993].¶The mass goes to zero as the boost goes to the speed of light, with the energy $E$ of the source held fixed [hotta1993]. The limit, published in 1993, is de Sitter space everywhere but on one null surface, $Z_0 + Z_1 = 0$ [hotta1993]. There the metric gains the term $\dfrac{4GE}{c^4}\left(\cos\theta\,\ln\dfrac{1 + \cos\theta}{1 - \cos\theta} - 2\right)\delta(Z_0 + Z_1)\left(dZ_0 + dZ_1\right)^2$, with $\theta$ the angle from the axis $Z_4$ [hotta1993]. That surface is a cosmological horizon, and at each moment the shock on it is a sphere [hotta1993]. The sphere keeps the area $4\pi a^2$ while the closed universe shrinks to its smallest size and grows again around it [podolsky1998impulsive]. Two massless particles ride it, one at $\theta = 0$ and one at $\theta = \pi$, each with the energy $E$ [hotta1993].¶Why two particles, when the boost began with one black hole? Written on the whole hyperboloid, the Schwarzschild-de Sitter field to first order in the mass has two point sources, at rest at opposite poles, and the boost sends both to the speed of light [hotta1993]. The same pair turned up from the other side in 1994, when Konstadinos Sfetsos extended the conditions under which Tevian Dray and Gerard 't Hooft could add a shock to a known solution, so that they cover backgrounds with matter and a cosmological constant [sfetsos1995, dray1985]. A single particle on the horizon of de Sitter space made him cut its shock off at the equator, and the simplest source that needs no cut is two particles of the same energy, one at each pole [sfetsos1995]. On crossing the shock a light ray is shifted along it, by an amount that diverges at each particle and changes sign $33.5°$ away from it [sfetsos1995].¶A metric with a delta function in it has to be checked by hand, and Hotta and Tanaka did so by extending Dray and 't Hooft's analysis [hotta1993, dray1985]. The shock passes on one condition, an equation for its profile $f$ on the sphere: $(\Delta + 2)f = 4\pi a^2J$, with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of the unit sphere and $J$ the energy of the sources per unit area, two delta functions for theirs [hotta1993]. Their interest was in gravitons: the invariant graviton propagator of de Sitter space was reported to diverge at long distance, which stood in the way of amplitudes for graviton exchange [hotta1993]. By 1987 't Hooft had pointed out that in flat space such an amplitude between two fast particles equals the amplitude for one of them to scatter in the plane shock wave of the other [thooft1987, hotta1993]. Hotta and Tanaka hoped their shock would do the same for de Sitter space, and in a second paper of 1993 they found that with quantum matter fields in the Euclidean vacuum the wave travels on without losing energy to particle creation [hotta1993, hotta1993quantum].¶Which shape can a wave front take if it cannot expand? The answer came in 1997 from Jiří Podolský and Jerry Griffiths, in several coordinate charts: in de Sitter space a sphere with a null particle at each pole, and with a negative cosmological constant a hyperboloidal surface of constant negative curvature carrying a single null particle [podolsky1997]. The particles need not be simple, and by 1998 Podolský and Griffiths had given them any multipole structure, with a profile that solves a Legendre equation on the wave front and Hotta and Tanaka's as its monopole [podolsky1998impulsive]. These waves are conformal to impulsive waves of Wolfgang Kundt's class, and for a negative cosmological constant they are impulsive limits of the waves of Stephen Siklos [podolsky1998impulsive, kundt1961, siklos1985]. With Roger Penrose's cut and paste the two built the same waves in 1999, slicing a space of constant curvature along a null surface and joining the halves again with a warp, in coordinates where $\Lambda \to 0$ is explicit and returns Aichelburg and Sexl's shock [podolsky1999nonexpanding, penrose1972impulsive]. Every geodesic followed in 2001, from Podolský and Marcello Ortaggio: a ring of free particles around the axis is focused onto it when the wave is strong enough, and spreads when it is weaker [podolsky2001].¶In de Sitter space the past of an observer never holds a whole Cauchy surface, though late in the observer's life it comes arbitrarily close [gao2000]. A slight perturbation changes that, by a theorem of 2000 due to Sijie Gao and Robert Wald: with matter that obeys the null energy condition, any observer at late enough times can "view the entire universe" [gao2000]. Two years on, Frédéric Leblond, Donald Marolf, and Robert Myers named such universes tall, since the conformal diagram grows taller than de Sitter's square [leblond2002]. For a shock in de Sitter space of three dimensions that obeys the null energy condition, Lars Aalsma and Gary Shiu found in 2020 that a geodesic crossing it comes out advanced, which brings the opposite poles into causal contact, "much like a traversable wormhole in Anti-de Sitter space" [aalsma2020]. With Alex Cole, Edward Morvan, and Jan Pieter van der Schaar they described in 2021 how information expelled through the cosmological horizon can reach an observer at the antipode [aalsma2021].

related.text: The limit $a \to \infty$, in which the cosmological constant goes to zero and the sphere flattens into a plane with one particle on it [hotta1993, podolsky1999nonexpanding].
Hotta and Tanaka boosted this black hole. The shock is its limit as the boost goes to the speed of light and the mass to zero, with the energy held fixed [hotta1993].
De Sitter space on either side of the shock. Cut along a cosmological horizon and joined again with a warp, it becomes this wave [podolsky1999nonexpanding].

The waves of anti-de Sitter space with plane fronts. The same boost done to the Schwarzschild-anti-de Sitter black hole gives an impulsive member of that family, with one null particle on a hyperboloidal front [podolsky1998impulsive].

coordinates.name: Conformally Flat

parameters.description: Energy of each of the two null particles, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as the mass $M$ of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole goes to zero and its boost $V$ to $c$
De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/a^2$; the wave front is a sphere of area $4\pi a^2$

coordinates.convention: We use Hotta and Tanaka's coordinates $(\eta, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, with the conformal time $\eta$ and the comoving radius $\rho$ both lengths, $\eta$ increasing to the future, and $\theta$ measured from the line joining the two particles. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Global Conformal

parameters.description: Energy of each of the two null particles, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as the mass $M$ of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole goes to zero and its boost $V$ to $c$
De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/a^2$; the wave front is a sphere of area $4\pi a^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\eta, \chi, \theta, \phi)$, all angles, with $\eta$ the conformal time, increasing to the future, $\chi$ the polar angle on the sphere $S^3$ of space, and $\theta$ measured from the line joining the two particles. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Null Cylindrical

parameters.description: Energy of each of the two null particles, the limit of $Mc^2/\sqrt{1 - V^2/c^2}$ as the mass $M$ of the Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole goes to zero and its boost $V$ to $c$
De Sitter radius, a length, fixed by the cosmological constant through $\Lambda = 3/a^2$; the wave front is a sphere of area $4\pi a^2$

coordinates.convention: We use the null coordinates $u$ and $v$, both lengths, with $\rho$ and $\phi$ polar coordinates on the stereographic projection of the wave front from one particle, which puts the other at $\rho = 0$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} + \dfrac{GE\left(16a^4 - 8a^2\,\rho^2 - 3\rho^4 - \left(12a^2\,\rho^2 - \rho^4\right)\ln\left(\dfrac{\rho^2}{4a^2}\right)\right)\delta(u)}{c^4\,a^2\,\rho\left(4a^2 + \rho^2\right)}\dot{u}^2 - \dfrac{2\rho}{4a^2 - uv + \rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{v} + \dfrac{2v}{4a^2 - uv + \rho^2}\dot{u}\dot{\rho} + \dfrac{2u}{4a^2 - uv + \rho^2}\dot{v}\dot{\rho} - \dfrac{2\rho}{4a^2 - uv + \rho^2}\dot{\rho}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(4a^2 - uv - \rho^2\right)}{4a^2 - uv + \rho^2}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
